motion: This House believes that urban sprawl is a damaging and unsustainable form of development that governments must actively restrain.

vocab.definition: A pattern of settlement in which daily life is almost impossible without private motor vehicles because of low density and separated land uses.
vocab.example: Car dependency locks households into high transport costs and leaves non-drivers isolated.

vocab.definition: The high per-person cost of providing roads, pipes, wires and services to low-density, spread-out development.
vocab.example: Infrastructure inefficiency means that sprawling suburbs often cost taxpayers more than they return in revenue.

vocab.definition: The breaking of continuous natural habitats into isolated patches by roads, housing and commercial strips.
vocab.example: Ecological fragmentation reduces biodiversity and weakens the resilience of local ecosystems.

vocab.definition: The growing distance between where people can afford to live and where jobs, services and opportunities are concentrated.
vocab.example: Spatial mismatch forces long commutes and reduces access to employment for lower-income households.

vocab.definition: The irreversible conversion of farmland, woodland and open space into low-density urban uses.
vocab.example: Rapid land consumption destroys productive agricultural soil and natural carbon sinks.

vocab.definition: The long-term gap between the cost of serving sprawling areas and the tax revenue they generate.
vocab.example: Many municipalities discover too late that new sprawl creates a permanent fiscal drain.

vocab.definition: The reduction in casual contact, walkability and shared public life that accompanies car-oriented, low-density layouts.
vocab.example: Social isolation is a hidden cost of designs that replace streets with private driveways and arterial roads.

vocab.definition: The extra greenhouse-gas emissions locked in by long travel distances, large heated buildings and extensive road networks.
vocab.example: Sprawl creates a lasting climate liability that denser development largely avoids.

vocab.definition: The way early low-density choices make later shifts to efficient, walkable patterns extremely difficult and expensive.
vocab.example: Once path dependency is established, correcting sprawl becomes a multi-decade and multi-billion-pound task.

vocab.definition: The progressive loss of countryside, views, quiet and local distinctiveness that residents themselves often value.
vocab.example: Amenity erosion turns the very qualities that attracted people to the urban edge into distant memories.

phrases.phrase: Sprawl externalises its true costs onto the public, the climate and future generations.
examples: Sprawl externalises its true costs onto the public, the climate and future generations while private developers capture the short-term gains.
Any honest appraisal must recognise that sprawl externalises its true costs onto the public, the climate and future generations.
We cannot continue a pattern in which sprawl externalises its true costs onto the public, the climate and future generations.

phrases.phrase: Low-density expansion is one of the most resource-intensive ways of accommodating population growth.
examples: Low-density expansion is one of the most resource-intensive ways of accommodating population growth and should be the option of last resort.
Evidence shows that low-density expansion is one of the most resource-intensive ways of accommodating population growth.
We should stop treating low-density expansion is one of the most resource-intensive ways of accommodating population growth as inevitable.

phrases.phrase: What looks like private freedom on the urban fringe becomes collective burden over time.
examples: What looks like private freedom on the urban fringe becomes collective burden over time in the form of congestion, pollution and higher taxes.
The long-term ledger reveals that what looks like private freedom on the urban fringe becomes collective burden over time.
Policy must confront the reality that what looks like private freedom on the urban fringe becomes collective burden over time.

phrases.phrase: Once the countryside is built over, it is gone for good.
examples: Once the countryside is built over, it is gone for good, along with its ecological and agricultural value.
The irreversibility is absolute: once the countryside is built over, it is gone for good.
We should act before the point at which once the countryside is built over, it is gone for good becomes the dominant reality.

phrases.phrase: Car-dependent layouts lock in inequality of access for anyone who cannot drive.
examples: Car-dependent layouts lock in inequality of access for anyone who cannot drive—children, the elderly, the disabled and the poor.
A just city cannot accept that car-dependent layouts lock in inequality of access for anyone who cannot drive.
The social consequences are clear: car-dependent layouts lock in inequality of access for anyone who cannot drive.

phrases.phrase: Restraining sprawl is not anti-housing; it is pro-efficient and pro-sustainable housing.
examples: Restraining sprawl is not anti-housing; it is pro-efficient and pro-sustainable housing that serves more people at lower long-term cost.
The distinction matters: restraining sprawl is not anti-housing; it is pro-efficient and pro-sustainable housing.
We can meet housing need once we accept that restraining sprawl is not anti-housing; it is pro-efficient and pro-sustainable housing.

idioms.definition: To destroy natural or valued landscape in the name of development and short-term convenience.
examples: Continued sprawl is simply the decision to pave paradise for another generation of low-density housing.
We still have time to stop paving paradise and to build differently.
The cultural cost of the urge to pave paradise is rarely entered in the developers’ accounts.

idioms.definition: An apparent saving that creates larger costs elsewhere or later.
examples: Cheap edge-of-town land is a false economy once the full infrastructure and transport costs are counted.
Sprawl repeatedly proves to be a false economy for municipal budgets.
We should stop mistaking short-term savings for a false economy that future taxpayers must service.

idioms.idiom: the thin end of the wedge
idioms.definition: A small initial concession that leads to much larger and less desirable consequences.
examples: Each new out-of-town permission is the thin end of the wedge for further countryside loss.
Relaxed planning on the fringe is often the thin end of the wedge.
Resisting the thin end of the wedge is easier than reversing decades of sprawl later.

idioms.idiom: kick the can down the road
idioms.definition: To postpone dealing with a problem, leaving it for others to solve later.
examples: Approving more sprawl simply kicks the can down the road on climate, congestion and infrastructure debt.
Responsible planning refuses to kick the can down the road.
Future residents will pay the price if we continue to kick the can down the road.

idioms.definition: A structure that appears stable but is in fact fragile and liable to collapse under pressure.
examples: The fiscal model of many sprawling suburbs is a house of cards once maintenance costs rise and growth slows.
Car-dependent prosperity can prove a house of cards when fuel prices or climate policy shift.
We should not build tomorrow’s communities on a house of cards.

idioms.definition: To solve one problem by creating or worsening another.
examples: Using greenfield sprawl to ease urban housing pressure is often to rob Peter to pay Paul with the countryside and the climate.
Short-term housing numbers achieved by sprawl merely rob Peter to pay Paul across the wider system.
Integrated policy refuses to rob Peter to pay Paul in the name of quick wins.

arguments.claim: Urban sprawl generates permanently higher greenhouse-gas emissions through longer travel distances and less efficient buildings.
arguments.explanation: Low-density, single-use development forces most trips to be made by private car and increases the average distance of those trips. Larger, detached houses also require more energy to heat and cool per occupant. Life-cycle analyses consistently show that sprawling metropolitan forms produce significantly higher per-capita transport and building emissions than compact alternatives. Once the road network and land-use pattern are fixed, these emissions become extremely difficult to reduce; electrification of vehicles helps but does not eliminate the extra vehicle-kilometres or the embodied carbon of extensive infrastructure. In a climate-constrained century, locking in high-emission urban form is a decision that future generations cannot easily reverse. Restraining sprawl is therefore one of the most effective spatial contributions a society can make to emissions reduction.

arguments.claim: The public cost of serving low-density development far exceeds the revenue it typically generates.
arguments.explanation: Roads, water, sewerage, electricity, broadband, schooling and emergency services all cost more per household when homes are spread thinly across the landscape. Studies from multiple countries show that the long-term municipal outlay for sprawling areas is higher than for compact neighbourhoods of similar population. New edge developments often appear profitable in the short term because initial infrastructure is subsidised or provided by developers, yet the replacement and maintenance burden falls on the wider tax base decades later. Many local authorities discover that the growth they once welcomed has become a structural fiscal drain. Continuing to permit sprawl without full-cost accounting simply transfers hidden liabilities onto existing residents and future taxpayers.

arguments.claim: Sprawl irreversibly consumes finite agricultural land and natural habitat.
arguments.explanation: Prime farmland and ecologically valuable land on the urban fringe are converted to housing, retail parks and roads at a rate that far exceeds population growth in many regions. Once sealed under asphalt and buildings, that soil and habitat are effectively lost for food production, carbon sequestration, flood management and biodiversity. The cumulative effect across a metropolitan region is the permanent shrinkage of the countryside that supplies food, recreation and ecological services to the city. Claims that ‘there is plenty of land’ ignore both the quality of the land being lost and the accelerating global pressures on remaining productive and natural surfaces. A responsible land-use policy treats the conversion of greenfield sites as a last resort rather than the default solution to housing demand.

arguments.claim: Car-dependent urban form systematically disadvantages anyone who cannot or does not drive.
arguments.explanation: Children, many older people, people with disabilities, and lower-income households without reliable car access face severe restrictions on mobility, employment and social participation in sprawling areas. Public transport is difficult and expensive to provide at viable frequencies when origins and destinations are scattered. Walking and cycling are often impractical or unsafe because of distance and road design. The result is a built environment that quietly excludes large sections of the population from full participation in urban life. Compact, mixed-use patterns restore a degree of independent mobility to these groups. Continuing to build primarily for the able-bodied car driver is a choice that embeds inequality into the physical fabric of the city.

arguments.claim: Sprawl undermines public health through reduced physical activity and increased pollution exposure.
arguments.explanation: Environments that make walking and cycling inconvenient or dangerous are associated with higher rates of obesity, cardiovascular disease and related conditions. Longer car journeys also increase population exposure to traffic-related air pollution and noise. While individual behaviour plays a role, the built environment sets the default options that shape daily movement patterns for entire populations. Evidence from public-health research consistently links more compact, walkable urban form with higher levels of active travel and better average health outcomes. Treating sprawl as a neutral or positive form of development ignores this well-documented pathway from land-use pattern to population health.

arguments.claim: Low-density expansion erodes the very amenity and character that attracted people to the urban edge.
arguments.explanation: Households often move outward in search of space, greenery and a sense of escape from the dense city. Successive waves of the same development replace fields and woodland with more housing, arterial roads and commercial strips. Within a generation the original attraction has been pushed further out or eliminated entirely, while the new residents face lengthening commutes and the loss of the rural setting they sought. This self-defeating dynamic is visible around almost every major city that has followed a sprawl trajectory. Planning restraint is not an attack on the desire for space; it is a recognition that unrestricted low-density growth destroys the spatial qualities it promises to deliver.

arguments.claim: Sprawl reduces the feasibility and efficiency of public transport and other shared services.
arguments.explanation: Viable public transport requires a critical mass of people living and working within reasonable distance of stops and stations. Low-density, dispersed development makes high-frequency services uneconomic and leaves residual bus routes slow and infrequent. The same logic applies to local shops, schools and health facilities: they either close or become reachable only by car. The outcome is a reinforcing cycle in which poor alternatives to the private car make car ownership feel essential, further reducing the customer base for shared services. Compact development reverses the cycle by making collective provision efficient again. Allowing sprawl is therefore also a decision to weaken the practical possibility of non-car mobility for decades to come.

arguments.claim: The claimed housing-affordability benefits of greenfield sprawl are often short-lived and incomplete.
arguments.explanation: Releasing large amounts of edge land can temporarily increase supply and moderate price pressure in some market segments. However, the new housing is frequently priced for higher-income households, while the infrastructure and commuting costs raise the true cost of living. Meanwhile the failure to redevelop under-used urban land and to permit gentle density in existing neighbourhoods leaves the more accessible locations still expensive. International comparisons show that cities which combine urban containment with active densification and social-housing provision achieve better long-term affordability outcomes than those that simply expand outward. Sprawl is therefore a partial and often temporary response to housing need rather than a structural solution.

arguments.claim: Path dependency makes sprawl exceptionally difficult and expensive to correct once established.
arguments.explanation: Road networks, plot sizes, building forms and household expectations all adapt to low-density, car-oriented patterns. Retrofitting public transport, enabling walking and cycling, or introducing mixed uses later requires costly reconstruction and faces intense local resistance. Cities that grew in sprawling form in the late twentieth century are now spending decades and large sums attempting to create more sustainable corridors and nodes. Preventing the pattern in the first place is far cheaper and more effective than trying to unwind it. The irreversibility of much sprawl development places a special responsibility on present planning decisions; each permission granted today narrows the options available to the next generation.

arguments.claim: A coherent response to housing need, climate targets and social equity requires active restraint of urban sprawl.
arguments.explanation: Unconstrained low-density expansion simultaneously worsens emissions, raises long-term public costs, consumes finite land, and embeds car-dependent inequality. Alternative approaches—brownfield regeneration, gentle densification of existing urban areas, transit-oriented development, and well-planned new settlements at higher density—can accommodate population growth while avoiding most of these harms. The technology, design knowledge and policy instruments already exist. What is required is the political decision to treat the open land around cities as a scarce resource rather than an endless development frontier. Restraining sprawl is therefore not an anti-growth posture; it is the precondition for growth that remains compatible with climate stability, fiscal prudence and equal access to urban opportunity.

vocab.definition: The ability of households to select the type, size and location of home that best matches their needs and preferences.
vocab.example: Housing choice includes the option of a family house with a garden on the urban edge when that is what people want.

vocab.definition: The demonstration through actual behaviour of what people value, such as the continued demand for lower-density living.
vocab.example: Preference revelation in housing markets shows sustained demand for space and privacy that dense urban forms often cannot supply.

vocab.definition: The responsiveness of new housing construction to rising prices; higher elasticity helps keep homes more affordable.
vocab.example: Greenfield development increases supply elasticity and thereby moderates price growth in high-demand regions.

vocab.definition: Residential environments that provide private outdoor areas, quieter streets and room for children to play safely.
vocab.example: Many families continue to seek family-friendly space that is difficult to deliver at high urban densities.

vocab.definition: The capacity of a city-region to grow, attract investment and create jobs, often supported by available development land.
vocab.example: Economic dynamism is harder to sustain when land-use rules make expansion prohibitively difficult.

vocab.definition: Planning rules and containment policies that limit the amount and location of new development.
vocab.example: Excessive regulatory constraint on the urban fringe is a major driver of housing shortages and high prices.

vocab.definition: The availability of different residential environments so that people can match their living situation to their stage of life and values.
vocab.example: Lifestyle diversity requires that lower-density options remain available alongside urban apartments.

vocab.definition: The gradual outward expansion of urban areas that has historically accommodated rising populations without sudden rupture.
vocab.example: Incremental growth on the edge has been the normal pattern of city development for generations.

vocab.definition: The widespread desire to own a freehold home with private outdoor space, which lower-density development is better able to satisfy.
vocab.example: Ownership aspiration remains strong and is more easily met through forms of development often labelled as sprawl.

vocab.definition: The ability of households and markets to adjust to changing transport technologies, work patterns and environmental standards.
vocab.example: Adaptation capacity means that today’s car-oriented suburbs can evolve with electrification and remote work.

phrases.phrase: Most households still express a clear preference for space, privacy and private outdoor areas.
examples: Most households still express a clear preference for space, privacy and private outdoor areas that compact urban forms struggle to provide at scale.
Survey after survey shows that most households still express a clear preference for space, privacy and private outdoor areas.
Policy that ignores the fact that most households still express a clear preference for space, privacy and private outdoor areas will face persistent resistance.

phrases.phrase: Restricting the supply of developable land is a direct cause of housing unaffordability.
examples: Restricting the supply of developable land is a direct cause of housing unaffordability in high-demand city regions.
The evidence links the claim that restricting the supply of developable land is a direct cause of housing unaffordability.
We cannot solve the housing crisis while refusing to accept that restricting the supply of developable land is a direct cause of housing unaffordability.

phrases.phrase: Urban containment policies often raise prices more effectively than they protect the environment.
examples: Urban containment policies often raise prices more effectively than they protect the environment or reduce emissions.
International comparisons suggest that urban containment policies often raise prices more effectively than they protect the environment.
A balanced view recognises that urban containment policies often raise prices more effectively than they protect the environment.

phrases.phrase: Technology and behaviour are already reducing the environmental impact of lower-density living.
examples: Technology and behaviour are already reducing the environmental impact of lower-density living through electrification, home working and better design.
The motion understates how far technology and behaviour are already reducing the environmental impact of lower-density living.
Future policy should build on the fact that technology and behaviour are already reducing the environmental impact of lower-density living.

phrases.phrase: One size of urban form does not fit every household or every stage of life.
examples: One size of urban form does not fit every household or every stage of life; diversity of provision is a strength.
Planning that insists one size of urban form does not fit every household or every stage of life is more realistic.
We defend the principle that one size of urban form does not fit every household or every stage of life.

phrases.phrase: The alternative to managed expansion is often more severe pressure and higher costs inside existing urban areas.
examples: The alternative to managed expansion is often more severe pressure and higher costs inside existing urban areas.
Those who oppose all fringe growth should acknowledge that the alternative to managed expansion is often more severe pressure and higher costs inside existing urban areas.
A complete analysis includes the reality that the alternative to managed expansion is often more severe pressure and higher costs inside existing urban areas.

idioms.definition: Opposition to new development close to where one already lives, even if one accepts the need for development in principle.
examples: Much of the resistance to new housing is classic not-in-my-backyard sentiment rather than a coherent anti-sprawl philosophy.
Urban containment can become a vehicle for not-in-my-backyard protection of existing homeowners’ amenity and asset values.
We should distinguish genuine sustainability concerns from not-in-my-backyard obstruction.

idioms.definition: A situation that combines the advantages of two different options.
examples: Many families seek the best of both worlds—access to urban labour markets and the space of a lower-density home.
Well-planned edge development can offer the best of both worlds when transport and services are properly provided.
Policy should aim to deliver the best of both worlds rather than force an artificial choice.

idioms.idiom: throw the baby out with the bathwater
idioms.definition: To discard something valuable while trying to get rid of something undesirable.
examples: An absolute ban on fringe growth risks throwing the baby out with the bathwater by eliminating legitimate housing choice.
We can reduce the harms of poorly planned sprawl without throwing the baby out with the bathwater.
Nuanced policy avoids throwing the baby out with the bathwater.

idioms.idiom: a rising tide lifts all boats
idioms.definition: General improvement or growth that benefits a wide range of people.
examples: Increased housing supply through a variety of forms can be a rising tide that lifts all boats on affordability.
Economic growth supported by adequate development land is often a rising tide that lifts all boats.
We should not dismiss the possibility that a rising tide lifts all boats in the housing market.

idioms.definition: To accept that others may choose differently and to refrain from imposing a single preferred lifestyle.
examples: A liberal approach to settlement form is to live and let live between those who prefer density and those who prefer space.
Forcing everyone into high-density living violates the spirit of live and let live.
Planning can set minimum environmental standards while still practising live and let live on density preferences.

idioms.definition: The real test of something is in its practical results rather than in theory.
examples: The proof of the pudding is that millions of households continue to choose and thrive in lower-density environments.
When people vote with their feet, the proof of the pudding is revealed in settlement patterns.
We should judge urban forms by the proof of the pudding—actual liveability and preference—rather than by abstract models alone.

arguments.claim: Large numbers of households continue to demonstrate a strong preference for lower-density living with private outdoor space.
arguments.explanation: Housing-market behaviour, stated-preference surveys and migration patterns all show sustained demand for family houses with gardens, quieter streets and a greater sense of privacy. This preference is especially strong among households with children and among those moving from apartments at certain life stages. Compact urban forms deliver many benefits, yet they do not fully satisfy this demand for a significant segment of the population. Preventing lower-density options in the name of anti-sprawl policy therefore overrides revealed preference rather than responding to it. A democratic planning system should accommodate a range of residential choices rather than treat one density band as the only legitimate form. The continued popularity of edge and suburban living is evidence that must be weighed alongside environmental critiques.

arguments.claim: Strict urban containment is a major contributor to housing shortages and high prices in growing city regions.
arguments.explanation: When the supply of developable land is tightly restricted, rising demand is forced into a limited stock of existing and brownfield sites. Prices and rents rise, younger and lower-income households are squeezed, and intergenerational inequality in housing wealth increases. Empirical work across multiple countries links tighter regulatory constraints on the urban fringe with steeper house-price growth. While densification inside the existing urban area is desirable and necessary, it has practical and political limits and cannot absorb all projected growth in high-demand regions. Managed release of greenfield land, properly planned and served by infrastructure, remains an important safety valve. Treating all fringe development as unacceptable sprawl removes that valve and intensifies the affordability crisis.

arguments.claim: Technological and behavioural change is already lowering the environmental cost of lower-density settlement.
arguments.explanation: Electrification of vehicles, improving public-transport connections to edge communities, remote and hybrid work, and higher energy-efficiency standards for new homes all reduce the carbon and congestion penalties previously associated with sprawl. Many of the most damaging features of twentieth-century car-dependent development are not inherent to lower density itself but to the specific technologies and planning practices of that era. New development can be required to meet stringent environmental performance standards, incorporate mixed uses, and reserve corridors for future transit. The environmental case against all forms of outward growth is therefore weaker than it was two decades ago. Policy should drive further improvement rather than assume that lower-density living is permanently incompatible with climate goals.

arguments.claim: Family life and child-rearing are often better supported by environments that provide private outdoor space and quieter streets.
arguments.explanation: Parents frequently cite the desire for a safe garden, space for children to play, and a less intense urban environment as reasons for moving outward. High-density living can offer excellent amenities, yet it also brings noise, limited private outdoor area, and greater reliance on shared facilities that may be congested or poorly maintained. For many households the trade-off continues to favour the lower-density option during the child-rearing years. Planning that systematically makes such options scarce or extremely expensive imposes a real welfare cost on families. A balanced approach maintains genuine choice so that those who value space for family life can still obtain it without having to leave the city-region entirely.

arguments.claim: Economic growth and job creation are supported by the availability of land for businesses and housing at reasonable cost.
arguments.explanation: Firms considering investment weigh the cost and availability of premises and the ability of employees to find suitable housing. Severe land-use constraints raise both commercial rents and residential prices, reducing a city-region’s attractiveness relative to more flexible competitors. Historical periods of strong growth have typically been accompanied by significant urban expansion. While growth can and should be steered toward more efficient patterns, an absolute presumption against fringe development risks choking off expansion and the employment that comes with it. The social costs of stagnant growth and extreme housing costs also deserve weight in the overall evaluation of anti-sprawl policies.

arguments.claim: Many criticisms of sprawl conflate poorly designed development with lower density itself.
arguments.explanation: Single-use zoning, hierarchical road systems that discourage walking, and the absence of local services are design and regulatory failures, not inevitable consequences of building at lower densities. It is possible to plan edge communities with mixed uses, connected street networks, green space and public-transport readiness. International examples of well-planned urban extensions demonstrate that expansion need not replicate the worst features of twentieth-century suburbia. Attacking ‘sprawl’ as a single phenomenon risks rejecting better forms of lower-density growth along with the worse ones. Precision in diagnosis allows policy to target genuine harms—car dependency, infrastructure inefficiency, habitat loss—without prohibiting an entire density band that many households prefer.

arguments.claim: Existing urban areas have limits to how much additional density they can absorb without eroding liveability.
arguments.explanation: Gentle densification is valuable and should be pursued, yet there are practical ceilings set by infrastructure capacity, heritage constraints, resident opposition, and the desire to preserve parks and character. Forcing all growth into the existing urban footprint can produce overcrowding, loss of family housing, and intense local conflict. Some cities that have pursued strong containment have seen sharp rises in inner-area prices and displacement pressures. A portfolio approach that combines urban intensification with carefully planned expansion is more resilient than an exclusive reliance on densification. Acknowledging the limits of the existing urban area is not a defence of uncontrolled sprawl; it is a recognition of real physical and social constraints.

arguments.claim: Ownership of a freehold house with private outdoor space remains a widely held and legitimate aspiration.
arguments.explanation: In many cultures the ability to own a house and garden is still regarded as a central marker of security and achievement. Lower-density development on the urban fringe has historically been the main route through which this aspiration is realised for middle-income households. Policies that make such housing extremely scarce or confined to the distant periphery effectively ration a valued good and concentrate its benefits among those who already own. While apartments and other tenures are essential parts of a modern housing system, they do not fully substitute for the ownership and space preferences of a large part of the population. A planning regime that treats those preferences as illegitimate or environmentally unacceptable risks deep and lasting public resistance.

arguments.claim: Adaptation and retrofit can improve the performance of existing and new lower-density areas over time.
arguments.explanation: Suburbs and edge communities are not frozen. They can gain better public transport, local service centres, protected cycle networks, and higher energy standards through successive waves of investment and regulation. Remote work has already reduced the necessity of daily long-distance commuting for many. Electrification will cut the local pollution and carbon intensity of remaining car use. The path-dependency argument is real but not absolute; incremental improvement is possible and is already occurring in many places. Writing off lower-density forms as permanently unsustainable understates the scope for adaptation and overstates the permanence of today’s technological and behavioural constraints.

arguments.claim: A pragmatic policy accommodates legitimate demand for space while enforcing high environmental and design standards on all new development.
arguments.explanation: The choice is not between uncontrolled sprawl and total containment. It is possible to release land for development in locations that minimise environmental harm, require mixed uses and active-travel infrastructure, impose strict energy and biodiversity standards, and recover the full cost of infrastructure from development. Such an approach respects housing need and household preference while addressing the genuine problems of car dependency, habitat loss and fiscal inefficiency. Absolute anti-sprawl orthodoxy tends to ignore the social and political costs of extreme scarcity. A more flexible, standards-based regime can deliver better outcomes on both housing supply and sustainability than a rigid presumption against all outward growth.
